meta.subtitle: A Memoir of Returning
meta.author: Jabooki Tanaka
meta.description: Letters, a diary and an interview: a family history told as a story, with the facts left where you can check them.

sections.title: A Note on the Text
sections.content:
This book follows the hybrid-narrative archetype: it reads like a story, but it does not ask you to take the story on trust. Dates, places and sources are signposted in the text, and every interruption is set apart so you can see where the narrator stops and a document begins.

Letters and diary entries are set as quotations, each with its source beneath it. Interviews are set as transcripts, the speaker named at the start of every turn. Notes stand at the foot of the page they belong to. Figure 1 is captioned where it falls, and the running text cross-refers to the Photo Plates that follow Part III.

sections.title: 1962 — Salt Road
sections.subtitle: Salt Road, the harbour town
sections.content:
My grandmother Hana did not write about the sea. She wrote about the road that led to it, because the road was the thing you could walk back along. The house at the end of Salt Road had one lit window in winter, and from that window you could see the tide come in and decide, twice a day, whether the town was an island or not.[^1]

I did not grow up in that house. I grew up with its letters. They arrived in bundles, tied with string, and my mother kept them in a drawer she never quite locked. When I finally opened them, forty years after the first one was written, I understood why she had kept the drawer unlocked: a locked drawer is a secret. An unlocked drawer is an invitation you are afraid to accept.

> “Dearest, — The tide was high at noon and the boats sat up on the sand like patient animals. Do not worry about the house. The house worries about itself, and it has more practice than either of us. Come home when the road is dry, not before.”
> — Hana Tanaka, letter to her daughter, 14 March 1962

That sentence — *come home when the road is dry* — became the rule of this book. I have tried to follow it. A memoir that hurries is a memoir that invents. A memoir that waits for the road to dry can at least say, honestly, what it found when it got there.[^2]

The desk was still there when I returned, and so were the bundles. Three of them, on the left of the desk, with the diary open between them as if someone had just stepped out of the room. I did not tidy it. Tidying is another way of editing, and I had already decided that this book would show its working.

![Hana's writing desk by a window: bundles of letters tied with string, an open diary and a pair of glasses](img:sr-desk "Figure 1. The desk at Salt Road, with Hana’s letters in bundles and the diary open. The bundles are shown in the order in which they were found, not the order in which they were written — that difference matters, and it is discussed in Part IV. Illustrative plate, not an archival photograph.")

Reading the letters in found order, rather than in date order, changes the story. In date order, Hana is steady, then tired, then steady again. In found order, she is tired first, and the steadiness that follows reads as a decision, not a temperament. I have kept both orders in the Chronology, so you can test that claim yourself.[^3]

[^1]: Hana Tanaka, letter, 14 Mar. 1962. Family papers, Salt Road drawer, Bundle 1.

[^2]: On waiting and invention in memoir, see the Note on the Text.

[^3]: Found order against date order: see the Chronology.

sections.title: 1987 — The Leaving
sections.subtitle: Salt Road to the city
sections.content:
My mother, Yuki, left Salt Road at nineteen, with one suitcase and a coat that was too thin for the road she was taking. She did not leave in anger. She left in the way people leave a house they love when the house has become too small for the life they can imagine. The town remembers the leaving differently from the way she does. That, too, is part of the record.[^4]

> “14 September 1987. I walked to the top of the road and looked back once. Only once. If I had looked back twice I would have stayed, and staying would have been a different kind of leaving.”
> — Yuki Tanaka, diary, 14 September 1987

When I interviewed the harbourman who watched her go, he did not mention the suitcase. He mentioned the coat.

::: transcript
INTERVIEWER: What do you remember about that morning?
HARBOURMAN: She was cold. She would not say so. She kept her hands in her pockets so no one would see them shake. That is how I knew she was not coming back that winter.
:::

::: right
*— Interview with the harbourman, Salt Road, 2024*[^5]
:::

[^4]: Yuki Tanaka, diary, 14 Sept. 1987. Family papers, Bundle 2.

[^5]: Interview with the harbourman, Salt Road, Mar. 2024. Transcript, sample file.

sections.title: 2024 — The Return
sections.subtitle: Salt Road, again
sections.content:
I returned in March, when the road was dry. The house was smaller than the letters had made it, which is the usual betrayal of memory, and larger than I had feared, which is the usual mercy of a place that has been kept. The harbour at low tide was the same shape it had always been, and the boats sat on the sand in the same patient order. See Plate I for the harbour at low tide, and Plate II for the road out of town.

Returning is not the opposite of leaving. Leaving is a single morning. Returning is a series of small negotiations: with a key that sticks, with a neighbour who remembers your mother better than you do, with a diary entry that contradicts a letter you have already quoted. I have left those contradictions in. A memoir that smooths them out is no longer a memoir; it is a story wearing a memoir’s clothes.[^6]

::: transcript
INTERVIEWER: Why come back now?
JABOOKI TANAKA: Because the drawer was unlocked. Because the letters were waiting. Because I finally understood that ‘come home when the road is dry’ was not an instruction about the weather.
:::

::: right
*— Interview with the author, Salt Road, March 2024*
:::

The road was dry. I came home. The rest of this book is an attempt to say, as plainly as I can, what home turned out to mean.

[^6]: Interview with the author, Salt Road, Mar. 2024. Transcript, sample file.

sections.title: What Remains
sections.subtitle: Salt Road, after the return
sections.content:
What remains is not the house, though the house remains. What remains is the habit Hana taught without teaching: write it down, tie it up, leave the drawer unlocked. I have tried to do the same with this book. The letters are quoted, not paraphrased into smoothness. The diary is quoted on the date it was written, not the date it would be most convenient to quote it. The interviews are quoted with their pauses left in, because a pause is also evidence.[^7]

If you read this book and feel that you know Salt Road, I have failed in one way and succeeded in another. You do not know Salt Road. You know the Salt Road that can be carried in letters, in a diary, in a harbourman’s memory, and in a daughter’s return. That is a smaller place, and a truer one, than any town you could visit. It is the only town a memoir can honestly offer you.[^8]

> “Come home when the road is dry, not before. And when you come home, bring the letters with you. They are heavier than they look, and lighter than you think.”
> — Hana Tanaka, letter, undated, found with the bundles

[^7]: On quoting pauses as evidence, see above.

[^8]: Hana Tanaka, undated letter, found with the bundles.

sections.title: Chronology
sections.content:
::: hanging
1962 — Hana writes from Salt Road; the house, the tide, the road.
1971 — Letters continue; the drawer fills.
1987 — 14 Sept.: Yuki leaves Salt Road with one suitcase.
1998 — Hana’s letters cease; the bundles are tied and kept.
2024 — Mar.: Jabooki Tanaka returns; interviews recorded.
2024 — The bundles are read in found order, then in date order.
:::
